lead: Parallel matrix transpose rearranges an n×n matrix a so that row i becomes column i. For every iparallel matrix multiplication.
prereq: You need: the PRAM and mesh models from Unit 1 and row-major storage of a 2-D array.

blocks.text: Take an n×n matrix a with row index i and column index j. Transposing a in place makes row i become column i. For every i<j, swap a[i][j] with a[j][i]. Diagonal cells a[i][i] stay. For n=3, a(0,1)=2 swaps with a(1,0)=4. Sequential in-place code reads the two cells of each pair and writes them back: n(n−1) reads and n(n−1) writes, which is Θ(n²). It performs no addition or multiplication, so arithmetic is zero and the whole cost is data movement.

On a PRAM with n² processors, give one processor to each cell. A processor at (i,j) with i<j reads a[i][j] and a[j][i], then writes the two cells swapped. Processors on the diagonal do nothing. All n(n−1)/2 unordered off-diagonal pairs act in the same step. The pair count is n(n−1)/2 because the diagonal is excluded and each unordered pair is counted once. Parallel time is O(1), assuming free routing. Work is n(n−1) reads plus n(n−1) writes, which is Θ(n²), the same as sequential, so the algorithm is work-optimal.

On a mesh, routing is not free. Place the n² cells on an n×n mesh, one per processor. A cell can move only to a neighbour in one step. A standard mesh transpose routes cells by row and column rotations: each cell walks along its row, then along its column, using offsets so no two cells collide. A cell travels at most 2n hops, so the parallel time is O(n). Thus the PRAM O(1) and mesh O(n) costs differ only because of routing, not because of extra arithmetic.

The blocked hypercube version works on blocks. Assume n = 2<sup>k</sup>. Cut the matrix into four n/2×n/2 blocks: top-left A, top-right B, bottom-left C, bottom-right D. The block transpose is [[Aᵀ,Cᵀ],[Bᵀ,Dᵀ]]. In place, exchange B and C with transposition: B becomes Cᵀ and C becomes Bᵀ; then transpose A and D recursively. Equivalently, swap B and C as whole blocks, then recursively transpose all four blocks. On a hypercube laid out so each block maps to a subcube, each recursion level exchanges two off-diagonal blocks between cube neighbours. There are k = log₂ n levels. The off-diagonal elements moved total n(n−1) = Θ(n²), so transpose is work-optimal. For general n, pad the matrix to the next power of two or handle uneven blocks.

spec.aria: The 3 by 3 matrix A and its transpose side by side, with the three swapped pairs shown in matching colours and the diagonal 1, 5, 9 unchanged.

examples.question: Transpose A = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]] on 9 PRAM processors, one per cell. List the swapping pairs and the cells that stay. Give the PRAM step count, the number of swapping pairs, and the total reads and writes.
steps: Use only pairs with i<j. Pair (0,1)-(1,0) swaps 2 and 4. Pair (0,2)-(2,0) swaps 3 and 7. Pair (1,2)-(2,1) swaps 6 and 8.
One processor handles each pair. Three processors swap in the same PRAM step, so parallel time is 1 step.
Each pair does 2 reads and 2 writes. Totals: 3×2=6 reads and 3×2=6 writes. The diagonal does no read or write in this scheme.
examples.answer: The PRAM transpose takes 1 step, uses 3 swapping pairs, and performs 6 reads and 6 writes.

traps: O(1) PRAM time assumes free routing. On a mesh the same n²-processor transpose takes O(n) steps.
Each unordered pair must be handled by exactly one processor. If both (i,j) and (j,i) write both cells, the cost doubles and races appear.
The diagonal never swaps. a[i][i] = a[i][i], so writing it again is redundant and can create a race.
The pair count n(n−1)/2 is not the work. In place, work is n(n−1) reads plus n(n−1) writes, which is Θ(n²); the pair count is half the off-diagonal cells.
Transpose is not matrix multiplication. There is no dot product; b[i][j] copies a[j][i].

quiz.q: Define the transpose of an n×n matrix.
quiz.a: b[i][j] = a[j][i] for all 0 ≤ i,j < n; rows become columns.

quiz.q: Why is transpose called a data-movement problem?
quiz.a: It does no arithmetic; cost is reading and writing cells. In place, n(n−1) reads plus n(n−1) writes, which is Θ(n²).

quiz.q: For n=4, how many unordered off-diagonal pairs swap?
On a PRAM with n² processors, how many parallel steps are needed when routing is free?
quiz.a: One step: all n(n−1)/2 pairs swap together.

quiz.q: Why does the same transpose take O(n) on a mesh?
quiz.a: Cells move one hop per step to neighbours; a row-column route needs at most 2n hops, so time is O(n). PRAM ignores this routing cost.

quiz.q: Is the PRAM transpose work-optimal? Give the work.
quiz.a: Yes. In place, work is n(n−1) reads plus n(n−1) writes, which is Θ(n²), the same order as sequential.

quiz.q: In the blocked hypercube transpose for n = 2<sup>k</sup>, how many block-exchange levels are there, and what does each level do?
quiz.a: There are k = log₂ n levels, assuming a hypercube layout matching the blocks. Each level exchanges the off-diagonal blocks with transposition (B becomes Cᵀ, C becomes Bᵀ) and recurses on the diagonal blocks A and D. For general n, pad or handle uneven blocks.

quiz.q: Why must the diagonal cells be left alone?
quiz.a: a[i][i] = a[i][i]; swapping it is redundant and can cause a double write or race.

beyond: Not for the exam. GPU transpose uses shared-memory tiles to avoid bank conflicts and to coalesce global memory reads; tuned kernels are in libraries. Distributed-memory transpose appears in FFT libraries, where an all-to-all exchange redistributes matrix blocks. Search for 'tiled matrix transpose CUDA', 'MPI all-to-all transpose' and 'cache-oblivious transpose'.
